utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yesterday it was foreshadowed that we would hear brief submissions about a couple of procedural matters. Mr. Moore, are you ready in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I am, thank you very much. Would you like me to start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, thank you. You cautioned us yesterday that we would have to announce any changes in our team. I am pleased to have this opportunity now to present my co-counsel, Mr. Vlado Domazet. He will be defending Mr. Mrksic with me. Thank you very much, Your Honours. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, thank you. We welcome your assistant co-counsel. I'm sorry, I had a pillar preventing me realising there was an additional co-counsel. Mr. Moore. Is that Mr. Lukic on his feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic has a problem with his microphone and the headset too. He's not receiving the right channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps he's not tuned in to the correct channel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is channel 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Channel 6, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no reception at all and the microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will make arrangements to get you on air as soon as possible, Mr. Lukic. It's not part of a scheme to shorten these proceedings that you are tuned out. I think you'll be able to -- will you be able to follow Mr. Moore in the meantime? Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have no objection to the -- what I'll call the daily bucket, disclosure of that, going to 48 hours. Neither have we any objection to the disclosure of that material prior to the evidence being given but we would ask that these two elements run hand in glove. In actual fact, I have an alternative submission. It's this: If there is going to be problems over authenticity of documents, it can work both ways. I have no problems at all working to a different timetable, which clearly would be within the inherent discretion of the court. If, for example, the Court was minded to do five days or seven days, we have considered it and we believe that with one small exception, we would be able to adhere to that criteria. So, for example, if the daily bucket was to be filled seven days ahead, and that material to be disclosed generally, all we would ask would be a discretion to be exercised benevolently by the Court that clearly there may be documents that will come in, for example, on proofing witnesses, through that seven days. The procedure that is adopted for the Prosecution is that witnesses will often come in three or four days prior to their testimony, and it might well be that some evidence has been given in court in the previous week that we had not anticipated and we would therefore wish to ask the witness whom we are proofing about that document. And therefore, we would clearly make an application to add that document into what I call the daily bucket. That is the only problem that I would actually foresee. So we have no objection to being extended. We have no objection to it being disclosed generally. And if the Court and my learned friends agree, I am working -- I am willing to work within a five day or a seven day time span.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. We will hear what other counsel have to say. Could I mention that we have been a little troubled by the language "daily bucket" and we think might try and use the language "daily folder" which is actually more accurate and less troublesome to sensitivities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with the daily folder, then, the weekly folder? The one matter that did concern us if I may just conclude my submission this way, is that it is not a criticism in any way at all against the Defence, they are entitled to put their case as they deem appropriate. But if there is going to be arguments about the validity or authenticity of a document, two days may not be sufficient to validate that document. Often we will have copies, let us say, from Zagreb or Belgrade. Often they are difficult to locate. If we work within an extended time span then that will certainly assist us rather than making an application to adjourn and conversely, if my learned friends are calling any documents that we have questions, then clearly we would be in a position to authenticate. In our submission, this is fair. It applies both ways and it will, I hope, stall the danger of application for adjournment. Those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Could I inquire, Mr. Lukic, whether you are yet on air? Thank you. Now, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence teams have agreed that Mr. Lukic will be the one to present our position on behalf of all the three Defence teams. I'm now passing the floor to him so that he can explain our position to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic. Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends. I will put forward several positions on behalf of all three teams. Some of my colleagues may decide to join me as we go along but our joint position is as follows: Related to two observations made by the presiding Judge Parker about allegations made in the pre-trial brief that the Defence, at least that's what the brief claims, will challenge the authenticity of a great number of documents. As far as we understand, we have not presented any such explicit positions. I wish to take this opportunity to inform the Trial Chamber that as far as the authenticity is concerned, the Defence will in fact be challenging rather few documents in relation to P65. This will be a small number of documents only and need cause you no further concern in terms of slowing down the E-trial procedure. As for the obligation of the Defence to disclose any documents to be used in cross-examination, and to hand this over to the Registrar, we believe it is quite sufficient for the Registrar to receive from us information on the documents that we intend to use within 24 hours prior to our examination. Then it will be of course up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether this time is reasonable. The question is whether to deliver these documents to the other party prior to our examination. I will here refer to paragraphs, not to Articles; this is paragraph 10 of the directive. The joint position for all three Defence teams is that before a witness is cross-examined, the Prosecution does not need to be served any of the documents likely to be used during cross-examination. First and foremost, we are pondering the meaning of E-Court as a system. We believe the meaning of the relevant directive is to expedite the proceedings and to make it easier for all the parties to use the comprehensive documents that are likely to be used during a trial like this. We do not believe that this directive is in any way compromised if no documents are in fact delivered to the other party before cross-examination. What really matters in terms of expeditiousness and general duration of trial is that the Registrar is given the relevant documents because the Registrar then passes these documents on to all the other parties and everyone in the courtroom. It is in this sense that the Defence has an additional interpretation of the Rules. In our submission, the rules are very specific about which documents and when are to be delivered to the other party, the Prosecution. And our conclusion is based on Rule 65, but the Prosecutor also faces the additional obligation under Rule 66(B) which does not apply to the Defence teams. This is the reason that the decision on reciprocal disclosure was abolished, a Rule that used to be part of the Rules. Were documents to be given, documents likely to be used in cross-examination, 24 hours ahead of time, and if at this point in time the party doing the examination-in-chief is still examining and this is likely to be the case very often, this would give the opportunity to the examining party to ask questions in relation to documents that the other party wishes to use. I think the whole point of cross-examination is for the cross-examining party to still be able to in a way surprise a witness and thereby question his credibility. The Defence believes that the fundamental principles of E-court will in no way be compromised if the other party is only served documents when the witness is about to be

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: rather, its second passage is perfectly clear. If we so agree, hard copies may as well be delivered to the other party when the cross-examination commences. But generally speaking, we believe that the principle of having private document lists, which is enshrined in paragraph 22, would be compromised in its entirety were documents to be forwarded to the other party ahead of time. We are perfectly aware of the fact that we will be facing the same situation when we start examining our witnesses, but then the same applies to all parties alike and the same applies to each and every instance that a party in these proceedings will be cross-examining a witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Could I point out that in the directive for E-Court, in Article 5, both Article 5(10), and Article 5(13) contemplate that the Chamber may order the time for release and, as Mr. Lukic has pointed out, Article 5(13) specifies as it were what will happen if no specific time has been ordered by the Chamber. And that is that, where the document is not released until the moment it is used in court, the party using the document, if it is a multi-paged exhibit, must have paper copies ready. What the Chamber is exploring, however, is whether it should order some time beforehand for the release of the document. Mr. Lukic, as we understand him, makes the point that that could disadvantage a party, whether it be Defence or Prosecution, in their cross-examination because they may lose the element of surprise in dealing with the witness. That, of course, could only be so if there was a disclosure to the witness of that document. What we had in contemplation was merely a disclosure to the Chamber and the other parties. If the witness was not then in the box, being in the course of giving evidence, there would be technically scope for the other party, when it first sees the document, to speak to the witness before the witness is called and mention the document. We recognise that as a possibility. So the issue is whether, in trying to determine how most efficiently and fairly to run the trial, there should be some earlier notice of the document to the other side. And in that, can I say the Chamber is encouraged to hear that the Defence at least contemplate challenging the authenticity of only a few documents. It may be that if that is the case, they will be in a position to let the Prosecution know at an earlier time of the documents that they question for authenticity, which will enable the Prosecution to obtain the original where that is possible, if it's not already to hand, and it will be possible, then, to look at the question of authenticity more readily. The fundamental position posed by Mr. Lukic is one as I'm sure all counsel appreciate, which is approached differently in different legal systems in the world, and one which is not specifically determined by the Statute, the Rules, or the directive in this Tribunal. It is a matter for assessment by the Chamber what will be most efficient and fair. The traditional common law approach was the one for which Mr. Lukic argues. That is, the document may be produced at the moment it is used and need not be known to the other party or the witness earlier. The traditional civil law approach requires the disclosure of all documents to the Bench at an early time, which is quite the opposite from the common law. In more recent years, there have been adjustments, particularly in many common law countries, to that procedure. And there is now, for example, both in England and Scotland and in federal jurisdiction in the United States, as there is in some parts of my own country, a procedure now which envisages earlier disclosure of documents. I say all that just to let you understand that the Chamber is well aware of the issues. We will look at the matter and probably announce our decision later in the course of the day. Thank you for your assistance. If there is no other procedural matter, we will arrange now for the witness to come back into court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just deal with one small matter for the witness? The witness has a broken ankle or heel and I've been told that she was feeling some difficulty yesterday because of pain. Keeping it in the same position causes her significant discomfort. I wonder if it's possible if she could have a short break perhaps after an hour, even if it's just for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think I did invite her to indicate yesterday if she was experiencing difficulty. We are well conscious of the injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This morning, as we have had necessarily a later than usual start, our working sessions will actually be just only a little over an hour each.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So I think we will by that means accommodate the problem today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will keep it in mind tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I indicate that the Chamber has had time enough to consider the matter now that has been dealt with in the submissions? We take the view that for the present, although we will keep the matter under review, for the present, we will not order any early disclosure of documents to the other party. We will order that 48 hours before a document is intended to be used, it will be released to the court Registry officer for inclusion in the confidential folder of that officer, but not that it be disclosed to any other party. And we will monitor whether that proves an efficient and effective system. In so doing, we are seeking to preserve what had been the position before the introduction of the electronic court system. I think that's all that need be said at this moment about that matter. Thank you for your submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I indicated yesterday, if you experience any particular discomfort with your injury, please indicate and we will adjourn or make whatever arrangements are necessary to help you. If I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, it still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to tab 20 of the same documents? And also tab 21?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the Court's leave I'm going to try to do it by date so we can move a little more quickly. So that is page 39 and 40, for tab 20. That is 65 ter number 223 and that's ZA002285, the B/C/S is ZA002285 also. And then tab 21 are pages 41, 42, they come from 65 ter number 996, the numbers there are 0117/2528, 2529.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to just look at, in your case, page 40. Really it is the same procedure that we dealt with in respect of phone calls yesterday. This reads, "From Dr. Bosanac", it's to the European mission, from Dr. Bosanac in Vukovar stated that today November the 2nd with aircraft from the air force and anti-aircraft Defence a bombardment was executed on the already-ruined hospital in Vukovar and the shelter and its vicinity. At that time in the hospital there were approximately 50 children and eight newborns are expected. As a result of the bombing, three casualties. Now, as I've already said the document is not something you have sent but looking at the content, can you recollect firstly whether you contacted anyone by telephone or any other means to inform them of such an event?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a telephone of the main Defence staff in Vinkovci. I had their telephone number and I informed them via telephone because that was the only communication link I had. I did not have a fax at that point. Rather, I made a phone call. And then I think they forwarded the message that I gave them over the phone elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to a bombardment, on the hospital, was it a case of it specifically being on the hospital or around the hospital? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They bombed the hospital and the area around the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move on, please, to tab 21? In your case, it's page 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you tendering that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was going to tender -- yes, I am going to tender. I was going to tender them collectively but I -- I can do that individually. My fault. May I make an application to tender that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, am I anticipating too much?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was wise of you to separate these two documents. As for the document marked 2285, it seems to be an original, whereas the document on page 40 is the translation into B/C/S. So it seems to be a transcript of a document in English, because it states here that there is a signature but we do not see one. Therefore, I ask that this document be marked for identification only so that we can establish what is the actual -- the original content of the document and then who translated it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it an MFI, Mr. Moore? Marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are so many initials at times one forgets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought that would have been an old Irish one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Regrettably not. Yes, please, thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification 20, not Exhibit 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we move on to tab 21? I've already referred for the record the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to look at page 41? And I will deal with the page 42. Can we please look at the bottom of this document that you apparently sent? It's dated the 2nd of November. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the people that you're sending it to, Admiral Brovet, President Tudjman, Minister Hebrang, General Tus and the EC monitor mission. Was it you who decided to send this letter or fax with copies to these individuals?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you choose these five nominated individuals?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was hoping that these five people could do something to stop the bombing of the hospital and further destruction and killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What effect was the bombardment having on the hospital and the people?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had a tremendous impact. People were dying. People died on that day. This man mentioned here was a handy man in the boiler room and he just went out of the boiler room when the shell landed and killed him on the spot. It was very difficult to work under those conditions, to maintain high spirits. People were scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through the details of the document itself. If we look at the final paragraph, the second sentence, certainly in English translation, "most urgently we are sending an appeal to the command of the JNA for a cease-fire." Was this the first time that you had asked for a cease-fire in relation to the, as you perceived, the attacks on the hospital and general area?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the first time. I sent such requests earlier as well. I asked that the attack -- attacks on the hospital cease. That was back in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could it I, please, for tab 21 to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we move on to tab 22? Tab 22 is at 65 ter number 996, the ERN number is 0117/2529. And 2530. The original document is 2530, Doctor, your page 43, top right-hand corner. This is the following day the 3rd of November, approximately two weeks before the capitulation of the Croatian defenders. May we just read this, please? "Vukovar is submitted to a severe attack." And then you go on to nominate aircraft, tanks, multiple-rocket launchers, large calibre machine-guns, and then in the previous day, 2nd of November, which we have just seen, 87 new wounded persons were brought to the hospital and 18 this morning. So "the number of wounded persons mostly civilians including women and children, has reached 350. The situation has become extremely critical. Medication supplies are almost exhausted. We are desperate. We are addressing anyone who can help us before it is not too late." May I deal with the second paragraph, please? The number that you were referring to reaching 350, you're saying that it is mostly civilians. Are you able, and I know it is difficult, are you able to assess what percentage of that 350 in the hospital were wounded civilians?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say this now looking back. However, I know that it was between 65 and 70 per cent. What I can say, based on what I remember from those days, is that civilians were mostly wounded in shell explosions and bomb explosions. These injuries were terrible. There had to be amputations of legs, arms. Young people and the defenders of Vukovar, Croatian soldiers, who at the time were members of the National Guards Corps and policemen mostly had firearm wounds through and through wounds, although that wasn't the sole injury that they typically had. Some of them also had injuries caused by shells. Those who were on the front line knew how to protect themselves, whereas civilians who went out of the hospital to get something, such as to repair a roof that had been destroyed the previous day, would normally be injured by shell explosions and those were extremely serious injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 22, may I make application for that to be made an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Moving on to 23. 23 is the day after, the 4th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's from 65 ter 223, and ZA002456, 2457, and 2458, the 4th of November. The original exhibit is at page 46, the translation, which is slightly unusual in its form, is page 45. Would you be kind enough, then, Doctor, please, to look at page 46? In that, there is reference clearly about urging international influence to stop the artillery and there is reference to the hospital. But again, I just want to move on to the bottom of that document, which really can be found at page 47. There seems to be a series of telephone numbers. Now, did you send this document or not? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the people that we see nominated clearly appear to be politicians, we have got Carrington, Major from Britain, Kohl from Germany and various other nationalities that don't need repeating perhaps. Why did you nominate those people to receive this correspondence?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had information that those were the people who at the time held important positions in Europe, and had a significant amount of influence that they could use in order to put an end to the war in Vukovar, to the shelling and the killing of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at the bottom of the typed copy, on page 45, there is a telephone message. For my part, I didn't check, I confess that, there is reference to a telephone message being received from Dr. Bosanac at 3.20 in the afternoon of November the 4th. It reads as follows, "Could you please add this to my letter sent to you today, the following: On this very day," i.e. the 4th of November, "in the last half hour, the hospital was hit over 90 times." That content, does that correspond with the recollection that you have for that day or not? That the hospital was hit 90 times and you asked for it to be added to the letter?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, I'd ask for tab 23, please, to be made an exhibit. I don't know if I have to read in the ERN numbers again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you assist the Chamber, Mr. Moore? The telephone message is on the English version. It does not appear on the B/C/S version. Are you able to clarify which was sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough just to help us with a query? If one looks at page 46/47, which is typed and clearly in B/C/S, we have the telephone numbers and the names of the politicians whom you wanted to have contacted. In the English translation, we don't have the telephone numbers but we do have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We do, if you turn to the second page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But not in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But if -- in the English translation, there is reference to your telephone call, which I've asked you about that. If one looks at the page 46 and indeed 47, is there any reference there to that telephone conversation? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had telephone numbers and fax numbers of the Croatian liaison office with the European monitoring mission, which was located in the hotel "I" in Zagreb. I sent my faxes there. I made phone calls there. And I asked them to forward my calls for help, both written ones and verbal ones, to these instances. There, in the Croatian liaison office, they translated both my written and oral cries for help into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to this document, I am concerned that we have not clarified something. On pages 46 and 47, we do not see the actual message. We only see it in the English version on page 45. So we don't know who received this message that was sent by the witness. And we don't know what is the original document here. I hope my learned friend could clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. It is still obscure, Mr. Moore. I suspect the effect of the evidence was that an e-mail or fax sent to Zagreb to the Croatian liaison office at the ECMM, who then sent letters reflecting the fax. If so, that leaves me a little confused as to the signature on the bottom of the B/C/S version. Or maybe the B/C/S version is the fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can add that lot into Mr. Vasic's problem and try and clear up some of the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of course, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we look at page 46, doctor -- if we look at a signature, please, at the bottom right-hand corner, at page 46, whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you contacted the liaison officer, was that by fax or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both fax and telephone. Different persons called back. I'm not sure who was in charge of the phone and fax machine at the exact time when I sent this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If one actually looks at page 46, and you look at the top left-hand corner, and I do mean the extreme left-hand corner, so go to page 46, literally the top of the page, there appears to be a date, 04/11, and then the number 91, and then 1421. But that's a little more difficult to read. Now, are you able to recollect -- and I know how difficult it can be -- clearly this is a fax that's dated the 4th of November. Can you remember when you sent it off, whether it was morning or afternoon or whether it was sent when it was dark? Are you able to assist?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say about this particular fax. I do know that I wrote most of the faxes in the morning or during the day, and I would have them sent immediately, but it's very difficult to say anything more specific in relation to this particular fax. These numbers that you can see at the top of the page, not clearly, are here because the faxes and the documents that we are talking about now are something that I received when I left prison and arrived in Zagreb. These were given to me by the liaison people with the ECMM. The original copies, the original documents, remained in the Vukovar Hospital following occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I would still make application for these documents to be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That was the 4th of November. May we move, please, to tab 24?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tab 24, pages 48, 49. Again it's to the European mission two days later, 65 ter number is 223, and the ERN numbers are ZA002454, 2456. I wasn't going to deal with this in any great detail, but can I just draw your attention, please, to halfway down the one paragraph itself? There appears to be in the translation, English translation, on page 48, "the whole town lives underground in shelters and basements." Can you find that particular part?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to explain to the Court what the living conditions were at that time that caused you to write that sentence?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions were difficult. There were 15.000 people still remaining in Vukovar. We organised these people around atomic shelters in residential buildings. However, there were far too few of those. There were other shelters around the town of Vukovar, in wine cellars, in cellars built under residential buildings. There was a shelter near the hospital, near a school building, and this cellar was quite solid. There was another one in Borovo Naselje, in the Borovo factory itself. In the factory building there were two shelters. One of them had been used as a small hospital, a small health station, where we brought patients. The whole town was living in its cellars because as soon as people left their shelter, they would immediately be casualties. There was no water and no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you refer to Borovo Naselje, again how far away is that from what I will call the Vukovar Hospital, in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About six or seven kilometres, thereabouts. I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to the injuries that you received at the Vukovar Hospital, let us deal with November, although I don't exclude other months, did you ever receive civilian casualties from the Borovo Naselje district and other districts?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, about two weeks before the fall, I can't remember the specific date but I believe you should be able to find it in one of the faxes, the road we refer to as Priljevo had been cut off. Therefore, those from Borovo Naselje could no longer reach the hospital. Rather, all the wounded had to go to the Borovo hospital where they also had doctors and nurses. They had to go there to seek help. There were other shelters too, in residential buildings, where we organised medical stations, with doctors and nurses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I apply, please, for the documents at tab 24 to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We just heard about the 6th of November. 7th of November at tab 25, 65 ter number 223. The ERN numbers are ZA002446 and 2453.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn to page 51 and we will deal with page 50. Again, it's a document that appears to have been faxed by you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's to the international mission and the United Nations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to deal with two or three areas of this particular document. Would you be kind enough, please, to go to the second paragraph? And it starts, "on many occasions the YPA aircraft discharged chemical weapons on the civilian population, of which we have material proof." Now, would you be kind enough, please, what it was that caused you to indicate that you believed that chemical weapons were being used on the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vesna Vukovic, a lady journalist, and myself wanted to use this letter to describe our daily experiences. This is something that we have already discussed, poison gases, smoke bombs, emitting fumes, chemical weapons. This is what we wanted to use the letter for. She said she would translate the letter herself and send the message across by using her radio station. As usual, I myself sent a copy of this letter to the ECMM asking them to forward the letter to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why do you refer to civilian population?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that's what the situation was. There were still 15.000 civilians in the town and the shelling continued on a daily basis, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And refer to the discharge chemical weapons of which you have material proof. What proof did you have that your belief that there were -- chemical weapons were being used?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we did have material proof. Bombs emitting various kinds of poisonous gases. We had preserved those in case members of an international organisation came to see us. We could use the samples to have them examined. Also, we preserved the clothes and boots of Silvana Ivankovic, the woman who had been injured, who had caught fire and smelled of phosphorus. We preserved these in the hospital in order to be able to use these items as proof some day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to those items that you had set aside for analysis? Did you retain them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The items were there for as long as we were there. I have no idea what happened to them later but I assumed -- I assume that the JNA soldiers, or whoever took over, also took these items away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions in relation to that document. Might I make application that the tab 25 documents become an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we move on to tab 26. The index is -- 53 should be 52, 52 should be 53, but apart from that it's correct. Page 52 relates to the B/C/S document 0117/2539. And the English is 0117/2540. They are from the 65 ter list at Exhibit 996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, can I just deal, please, with page 52, as I have it? Which is the original document. Is that your signature at the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: For the Court's assistance because it doesn't show on the translation, if one looks down the core of the document, on the right-hand side, what I will call 4.00, is that right that there are other signatures on the original document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are three signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And whose signatures are they, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the signatures of the wounded JNA soldiers who were receiving treatment at the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. They don't show on the transcription. Can we deal, then, please, with this document, how it arose, and how the signatures were added to it? We can see that today is the 7th of November and there is reference to throughout the entire day, "the hospital has been the target of the fiercest artillery assault." Do you see that part, the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, if I just move on in general terms, what you say basically is that there is a continuing attack, that there are wounded JNA soldiers, who have by your phrase pur chance survived, and you ask for urgent cease-fire and the withdrawal of the JNA from the municipality. Now, I'd like to deal with the reference to what I will call Mr. Raseta, and it reads as follows: "For the verification of the truthfulness for Mr. Raseta and others that are responsible for this massacre on the hospital, I ask the wounded JNA soldiers to confirm with their signatures." And then we have got three names, that they are two soldiers, one is a reservist and actually where they came from.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you adopt this approach of asking for JNA soldiers to add their name and the signature?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was some sort of hope for me. I reckoned if Raseta was not inclined to believe me, maybe he would believe them because they were, after all, JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, who was Raseta? Who did you believe he was and what was his influence as you perceived it to be?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I knew him to be a representative of the JNA in Zagreb. I knew that he was the officer negotiating with the Croatian government, negotiating a cease-fire, negotiating about convoys. That's all I knew at the time. I knew he was a general by rank and his name was Andrija Raseta. That was all I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with the three soldiers themselves? How did it arise that three JNA soldiers came to add their signature to this document, asking or confirming that such an attack was occurring? Can you explain to the Court how it arose?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this day, as on any other day, there were shells and bombs falling on the hospital. On this particular day, however, a shell hit the room where these soldiers were, or, rather, a room which at the time was being used by a dentist, Zeljko Gottfried. The shell demolished two of the room's walls. I personally went there to see if the people in the room were still alive. We pulled them out of the room. And after that, they were together with all the other wounded and patients in the hallway that you saw in the footage that you showed yesterday. I asked them myself if they were willing to help and sign the appeals that I was sending out. I said this would give us better hope and that maybe the JNA would believe us, since they didn't seem to believe me. All three of them agreed and signed the document. I asked them if they wanted to speak to Raseta on the phone. They said they were glad to do so. This soldier named Sasa picked up the phone and spoke to Raseta from my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to Sasa Jovic, you were present when he was speaking or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What sort of things was he saying to General Raseta?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He introduced himself to General Raseta. He said his name was Sasa Jovic, that he was in the Vukovar Hospital, and then Raseta asked him if he was the only JNA person there. He asked him who was in the hospital? He said there were many wounded there. Raseta wanted to know about the wounded Croatian soldiers in the hospital, and the soldier told him that there were no soldiers there but, rather, just the sick and wounded and that shells and bombs were falling on the hospital. It was a brief conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And after the conversation, did you speak to General Raseta?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I want to just deal with this day, after Sasa Jovic had spoken to Raseta. Can you remember if you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to him then. I pleaded with him to tell them to stop shelling the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as a result of this conversation with Jovic and yourself, did Raseta say anything down the telephone to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he would see what he could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And thereafter, in the days that followed, did the bombardment cease on the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with one aspect of your evidence? You have said that Raseta had asked Jovic about Croatian soldiers at the hospital. We know from your evidence that the upper parts of the hospital were in a very bad state. We have seen photographs as well. To your personal knowledge, was that hospital used by the Croatian soldiers in any military way?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is one thing that I know for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say you know it for certain, how do you know that for certain?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was there every single day. I would arrive at 6.00 in the morning and I would stay until as late as 2.00 or 3.00 a.m. I was all over the hospital. I would go from attic to cellar, the new building, the old building, including the hospital yard. I would certainly have noticed that the hospital was being used for any sort of military purpose, or I would have heard this from someone. I am, however, certain that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will ask for the documents at tab 26 to be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be Exhibit number 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, that is probably a convenient time for a break, and it will allow Dr. Bosanac to move her leg. We will resume at 20 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I just ask the witness, please, to turn to tab 27, page 55, for her, but I would just like to clarify one matter for whether -- before proceeding, whether we would be seeking to rely on this document or not. I just wish to authentic the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to look at page 55? Do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the handwriting of my colleague who admitted Silvana Ivankovic. This is her medical history where it is described that she is being admitted into hospital, the findings upon examination are listed here, the examination of the entire body, as well as pertinent injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, my microphone or translation was not operating at the time. It's now repaired. Would you be kind enough, please, just to give me a moment and I can check what the -- what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I deal with did in this way, that we already have got tab 28, which as yet has not been made an exhibit? I would be moving on to tab 28. I believe that there is no objection to that, to some extent it's duplication. It deals with the same witness. And as such, I wouldn't be seeking to put it in as an exhibit, as we would be moving on, as I say, to the following number, tab 28. So unless there is any objection to that course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we ignore tab 27?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. To some extent it duplicates firstly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not to some extent. We either ignore it or we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We ignore it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we move on, please, to tab 28? That is a document that we've already dealt with. And I seek to make that a Prosecution Exhibit. I made an application earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We had marked it for identification as 28, because you didn't tender the last exhibit. We will not have a 27 or this will become 27? Which is your preference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it's a conundrum. Tab 27 is technically relevant. Of that there is no doubt. What it is is quite simply a duplication of Ivankovic's material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I just a suggestion? Marked for identification, tab 27, as 27. Don't tender it. And then we can forget it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then move to this one as Exhibit 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, that's an excellent idea. Thank you. May we move on, then, to tab 29?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just let the court officer catch up. Tab 27 will be marked for identification as 27, and that which is marked for identification as 28 from yesterday will now become Exhibit 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we move on, then, to tab 29. Tab 29 relates to a report from the hospital. This is the 9th of November. Page number 62. The English translation is 0117/2541 and the B/C/S version is 65 ter number 223, and it's 0117/2541.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn up page 23 -- sorry, page 63? And I will deal with page 62, the English translation. If we look at page 63, there is a signature at the bottom of that page. Can you confirm if that is your signature or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal, then, please, with this document? Basically, it rehearses the level of damage, a baby being born prematurely. You refer to situation being exceptionally serious, constant fire against the hospital walls and roof, and there is no water. May I deal, please, with the fires on the roof and the consequence for the hospital at that time? Can you recollect when it was that the fires were on the walls and roofs?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on the date, the exact date or do you mean at a certain time during the day? What happened here happened in the afternoon, as is stated in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us, please, then, about the fires that happened in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two incendiary shells landed on the roof of the hospital. I was informed by my associates who were outside at the time that the roof was on fire. Then I went upstairs with my associates. We went up to the roof to see the extent of the damage. We saw that between the roof and the walls of the hospital, there was a fire in progress. Then I asked my associates to bring as much water as they could up there, and dump it on the fire, but to be careful so that the others in the hospital would not notice their activities, other workers, patients and so on, so that they wouldn't panic. Fortunately we managed to contain the situation. We poured water on the fire and put it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then finally this: The final paragraph relates to the 8th of November, the previous day, and there is reference to 75 new wounded. And a reference to 35 operations being performed on that group. Again, are you able to assist the Court about the percentage of those people who were arriving, how many were civilian? Or apparently civilian?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say now, but the usual would apply in this case as well. Usually 60 to 70 per cent of all admitted into hospital were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I apply, please, for the tab 29 documents to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that with respect to this document, there are two problems. The first one is that we do not know to whom this document was transmitted. My learned friend omitted to ask this. The other problem is that on page 62, at the bottom of the page, there is a PS notation indicating the 10th of November 1991, whereas in the heading, the date listed is the 9th of November. Therefore, it is not entirely clear when this document was composed and by whom and to whom it was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy to deal with those objections or concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Who -- to whom was this document sent, doctor?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent to the Croatian liaison with the European mission, as were all the previous documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you look at your page 63, there is reference, post scriptum in English, although it's not English, the 10th of November, we are still alive but not for long, it would seem. Do you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember -- and it's dated, of course, the 10th, not the 9th. That's the point. Do you know who added that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I added that, or, rather, my clerk, to whom I dictated this text. We wrote the text in the afternoon on the 9th. I didn't send it immediately by fax on that day but, rather, on the following day, on the 10th. And before it was sent by fax, we added this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I hope that deals with all the concerns of my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on, then, please, to tab 30. We are moving on to the 11th of November. The tab 30 documents, 996, is a 65 ter number, and 0117/2542, 0117/2543 are the B/C/S ERN numbers and the English is 0117/2547.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn to page 64 and 65 which are the B/C/S version? And I have got an English translation on the -- page 66. Dealing with this, please, who was it sent to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was sent once again to the European mission, to the Ministry of Health, namely to Professor Hebrang but in view of the fact that I was unable it go and send the fax personally, I simply sent it to the post office, and it was sent to the Osijek post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Clearly I have been asking you questions through this period about faxes. We also know that you had a telephone and we know from evidence you gave before the break about a telephone call to General Raseta. If we deal with November, and I know it's difficult to particularise, but how often would you be using your telephone to contact individuals in relation to the JNA or, if I may use that phrase, the Serbian position?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second half of November, I called every day asking to be connected to the Main Staff, the office of admiral Brovet and to General Raseta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you did that, did you have any success in communicating with them or any of their staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I managed once to speak to somebody. I don't know to whom. Who was a member of the General staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what did you say to them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them who I was. I said that I was calling from the hospital in Vukovar, that I was director of the hospital, and that I was asking them to stop shelling Vukovar and the hospital and to stop the air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did it have any success at all?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In this letter, you deal with the fact, as you calculate it to be the 81st day of the blockade of Vukovar. Now, that is the first line and you refer to the 81st day of intensive artillery and aircraft fire referring to civilian buildings. Where do you -- I use the phrase Rubicon, where do you say the Rubicon was, or where was the line of when Vukovar was being blockaded because you use 81 days. From what date are you working?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We started counting that from the 25th of August, when almost all roads were cut off, all roads leading to Vukovar. At the time, there was just one road left, a rather risky one, through Luzac and through the corn fields. That was operational in September. And occasionally, the wounded were evacuated via that road. However, as for the regular supplies, with food, with medication and so on, that was disrupted from the 25th of August on, and we considered ourselves to be under siege. So therefore 81 days was counting from that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to go into paragraphs 1 and 2, where there is numbers mentioned. But I'd like you to deal, please, with an incident that you refer to here on the 11th of November in respect of five heavily wounded persons, of which three have cranial cerebral injuries and you actually make the distance of five kilometres to the hospital. Where had those people been brought from? What district?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were brought in from Borovo Naselje. At the time, the road was cut off. The tanks entered through Luzac. The street that we called Priljevo which connects Vukovar to the -- to Borovo Naselje, and these people were brought by other people from Borovo Naselje to the hospital. They carried them physically in their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My I make application that the tab 30 documents be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tab 31. Tab 31, pages 67 and 68. These are telephone messages. They are from the 65 ter number of Exhibit number of 223. ZA002440 and 2441.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you look at page 68, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I think there may be an error on page 68 index because I see it says English and it's clearly not English. So page 67 seems to be the translation. I will have that clarified. Page 68 seems to be the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So, doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn to page 68? If we look at that particular document, there appears to be your name. Is that right? Bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's directed to whom?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the European mission in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The English translation refers to November the 13th at 1600 hours but even from my untrained eye it's clear that the B/C/S is not that time. It's 1620. But perhaps if I can deal with the content for a moment. May we just look, please, at one or two parts of this document? If one moves down to the fifth paragraph, which starts, "We are inviting all the responsible members," it's under number 2. Do you see that, doctor?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We are inviting all the responsible members of the European mission and UNICEF, as well as other organisations who wish to help to visit Vukovar afterwards and witness by themselves the massacre upon the population of Vukovar, regardless of nationality. Why do you use the phrase, "massacre of the population of Vukovar, regardless of nationality"? What was it that you saw or are aware of that caused you to use that phrase?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those three months, I saw quite a lot. A lot of people who were killed by shells, bombs, people without extremities, without heads. People of all ethnic backgrounds. The victims came from all groups who remained in Vukovar. People were killed, houses were destroyed, and this is something that prompted me to write this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't wish to ask any more questions on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd ask it to be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid we have once again two problems. This time they both pertain to the English translation. In the B/C/S version of the document, therefore the official version, below the signature of the witness, it says, "Vukovar November 1991." This portion is missing from the English translation. And in the text itself, it says, "Out of 14 newly admitted wounded patients on the 13th of November," that was translated into English as the 12th of November. In transcript on page 37, line 20, it should say "Vukovar, the 13th of November 1991."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, and also in the heading, the time it appears should be 1620 rather than 1600.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. But I believed that that issue was already raised by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those matters seem self-evident, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Those matters having been noted in the transcript, the document will be received as Exhibit 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tab 32. 14th of November, four days before the surrender of Vukovar. Page 69, page 70, document going to the European mission, in B/C/S it is 65 per number 996, ERN number 0117/2550 and 2551.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn to page 69? We will deal with the English translation. Again bottom right-hand corner, appears to be Dr. Vesna Bosanac, and in Vukovar, 14th of November 1991. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's to the European mission. Can we just clarify certain parts again of this document? "We are informing you that today on the 14th of November, 1991, the situation in the Vukovar Hospital is getting more and more difficult, considering there are 12 new wounded that have been admitted to the hospital yesterday and there is no water in the hospital, food supplies are getting scarce, and we are running out of medicaments," and then you refer to injuries and other matters of which I'm not going to deal with. Would you go, then, please to the bottom or the final paragraph, "protect, gentlemen, at least the children of Vukovar. Among the wounded, among which there are 70 per cent of civilians, the gaseous gangrene is in process and we cannot say for how long we will be able to survive. We are once again asking you for peace and for the withdrawal." Now, this has gone again to presumably the Croatian liaison officer at the European mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you receive any reply, not only to this document, but to the other documents that you had repeatedly been sending to the missions, asking for assistance for the hospital? Firstly can we deal with this in general terms and then specific terms? So what replies were you getting, if any?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received no reply whatsoever. I only had telephone conversations with Minister Hebrang who promised help to me informed me about the fact that there were negotiations going on, about cease-fire, and evacuation. However, I received no written reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any telephone contact from the European missions in respect of these faxes that you sent?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only thing I received was on the 18th. That was the day when they were supposed to come to Vukovar but failed to appear. That was when I received a note via telephone from the European monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that in a moment but if I may at this time, then, not ask any further questions in respect of tab 32, make application for the tab 32 document to be Exhibit 32?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we move on to tab 33? Tab 33 is down as a message from yourself on the 15th of November, ter number 996, and the ERN number is 0117/2552.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, doctor, to turn to number 71, page 71? The English version is on page 72. Is it right, we see your name at the bottom right-hand corner? Do you remember sending this document or note?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, message.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It was a message. Well, the way it starts is dear sirs and it concludes with, "Sincerely." Can you remember whether it was a document that was faxed? If we look at page -- well, you have to do. Look at page 71. Who typed this? Or where was it typed, is a better question.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say right now. I know that I dictated this document to someone but I'm not sure if the original was sent or a copy. This is not something that I can say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we deal with the -- with the content, perhaps we can ascertain whether in actual fact you identify the document. Today the 15th of November, we address you from the Vukovar Hospital. Would you be kind enough, please, to read it to yourself and see if you can identify the contents as being the contents of which you created and then subsequently dictated?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that I was the one who dictated this, and I'm able to identify this as the letter that I thought up and then dictated to someone. The only thing I am unable to say is, in view of the fact that the document is not signed, whether this was the very document that was produced when I dictated it or whether this is in fact a copy of the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Might I draw your attention, please, to the third paragraph standing -- starting "we demand that you fully exercise your influence to stop the war, get the Yugoslav army to withdraw from Vukovar." I'd like you to deal with the next part. "Lift the roadblocks to enable transport of food and medicine and allow for repairs of the water pipeline in order to prevents infections and an epidemic." Now, the roadblocks and the transportation of food and medicine, to what extent were you able to obtain medicine and/or food in that last period of November, before the surrender?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation with water was extremely difficult. We used the surrounding wells. We collected rain water. The same applied to food. We were given some food from the Red Cross and Caritas storage, mostly canned food, flour. We had nothing to use in order to make bread, so the bread we ate was the hard kind of bread, not the soft one. Medicine was running short too, but we did receive assistance on several occasions. There were planes from Osijek flying over Vukovar at night and they would drop military parcels with blood and the medical necessities. There were two such parcels that were brought to the hospital on the last days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've mentioned the Red Cross. Where was the Red Cross coming from?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross was operating inside the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you have any significant help coming into Vukovar across the roadblocks? Are you able to assist with that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's the way I phrased the question, it was badly put. Is it a case that you did not receive assistance or you can't remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received none. I know that. On the very last days, there were these airplanes that were dropping these parcels with medicine and blood reserves, but no food or any other necessities got through the blockade, since the beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I apply for the tab 33 document to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We still don't know who this document was sent to. The only thing that the heading indicates is "from Dr. Vesna Bosanac," but there is another concern I wish to raise about this document, the way it was typed up. If you have a look, all the documents that we have already tendered, documents of the medical centre or leaving the medical centre, were typewritten. It would seem that the case of this document is not consistent with the other cases. It was computer typed, apparently. At the point in time under consideration, I don't think the witness was able to have a document typed up on a computer. This raises some serious doubts concerning the authenticity of this document, particularly whether the document was actually produced by the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you wish to pursue that any further, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes we would have two submissions. The first would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Submissions or questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was going to deal with submissions in relation to the objections, and then I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The submissions are very short. They would be quite simply this: Firstly that the doctor has said repeatedly that she has always sent faxes to the liaison officer at the European Commission. My understanding was that she distinguished, if that was not the case. The second is simply this: That in our submission, page 31, the type script surely is a question for cross-examination, and therefore, if there is any concern, it can be marked for identification and can be cross-examined on. Those are the only submissions I would make on those concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So do I understand that you propose that it be marked for identification at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm perfectly happy for it to be marked for identification but on the basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Page 71 I think the transcript notes was 31 which may have been what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Could I indicate, Mr. Vasic that the Chamber's understanding of the evidence of the witness is that each of these documents was sent by fax to the Croatian liaison officer at the European mission in Zagreb, unless she has specifically indicated otherwise, and on that basis, we would receive the document. In view of your concern about authenticity, Mr. Moore has indicated he will only move it to be marked for identification until after you've had a chance to cross-examine. So we will mark it for identification on that basis as 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I move, please, to tab 34? Tab 34 is a document, 65 ter number 996, ERN number 0117/2553.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn up page 74? And 73 appears to be the original. Now, can I just deal with this document? It's right, I think, that it has the heading of the medical centre of Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the message was accepted on the 18th of November, apparently at 8.50 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to just deal, please, with the content of this message. It's originally sent to the apparently the European mission and is headed urgent protest. Would you be kind enough, please, to read the content of that document and confirm whether in actual fact it corresponds with a message you may have sent to the European mission itself on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who did you send it to, or let me rephrase that? Who did you telephone about this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the liaison officer with the Croatian office of the European mission in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So this is the 18th of November, ten to 9.00 in the morning. It reads as follows: "The tanks are still continuously firing on the hospital. There are 600 patients and as many civilians at the hospital in this moment awaiting the evacuation. We are asking for urgent evacuation. The patients and the civilians are supposed to the tank fire, hunger and thirst. We are appealing to the EC mission to urgently come to the hospital." And then you indicate they can safely pass through Luzac. Now it may be a case of translation, and if it is, please inform me. But can I deal, please, with the first paragraph? Because it says there are 600 patients, as many civilians, at the hospital at this moment awaiting the evacuation. Not "an" evacuation, but "the." Now, were you at this time expecting to be evacuated? Or was it a case of hoping to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were expecting, according to the information I had, on the 18th of November, at 8.00 in the morning, two teams were supposed to arrive. Two Red Cross teams were supposed to arrive at the Vukovar Hospital, one from Ilok, across Mitnica to Vukovar and the hospital, and the other across the Danube by ship from Backa. The European monitors were supposed to arrive too so that the hospital evacuation could commence, which had been agreed by the European monitors in Zagreb. Instead, the tanks opened fire again. It was at this point in time that I picked up the phone again and lodged this protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just then deal with your evidence for a moment? You said that you were expecting two Red Cross teams, one from Ilok, one across the Danube. Who informed you that there would be these evacuations? When did you find out?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister Hebrang, on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where was Minister Hebrang at that time, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, what was your information that Minister Hebrang was doing in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was involved in negotiations concerning the evacuation, alongside with the International Red Cross, and General Raseta, who was representing the JNA. They wanted me to give them the total number of wounded, those seriously wounded, who required evacuation by an ambulance. The number of personnel and civilians in the hospital, information which I had provided on the previous days. On Sunday, the 17th, I was told that next Monday, on the 18th, representatives of the International Red Cross and European monitors would be arriving in the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know what terms were going to apply for this evacuation? What were the rules for the evacuation of the people from Vukovar and the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
