utterances.text: What do you mean by rules?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What did you understand would be the guidelines for the evacuation? Who was going to do what? Who was going to be present where?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to prepare the wounded, to determine how many ambulances would be needed and how many seats on the buses, so in addition to that, they discussed evacuation routes, of which several had been envisaged. They asked me which I believed was the easiest and the simplest route to use. I told them it was the same route that had been used by the convoy, when the Medecins Sans Frontieres first came in. This was the route from the hospital across Luzac through Bogdanovci, Marinci, and Nustar. I was told by Minister Hebrang that this route would indeed be used for the evacuation, that those most seriously wounded, as well as the hospital personnel would be evacuated along that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: On an earlier occasion you had asked for an evacuation to be under the control of three parties. The first was JNA, the second was Croatian forces and the third was monitors. Who was going to be controlling this particular evacuation? What was your understanding in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was the same in relation to this evacuation, that it would be monitored and that it would be conducted by the International Red Cross, with the monitoring of the European monitors obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How important was it to you to have the European or any monitors participating in the evacuation at this time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very important, exceptionally important, to me and to all of us in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say why it was exceptionally important to me. The reason was that I had no reason to expect that the evacuation would be swift and effective unless the European monitors and the International Red Cross were present, considering everything that we had been through up to that day, the 18th, our fear was great. Our concern was great about the progress of the evacuation that was in the offing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was your fear only towards speed or was it affected by other concerns?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our fear was about the Yugoslav soldiers who had spent most of their time up to that point demolishing the town and killing people. We were afraid of what would happen once they reached the hospital in the absence of the European monitors and the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever inform any person of your fears for the safety of many of the patients, in respect of the behaviour of the JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who did you tell of this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed Minister Hebrang. We spoke and my colleagues also spoke to him, for hours during those last few days. We spoke about how we would organise the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about the -- expecting two teams of Red Cross to come on the 18th. Did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When they didn't arrive, did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I phoned minister Hebrang again, and I also phoned the Office for Cooperation with the European mission in Zagreb. Minister Hebrang replied by saying that he would look into the matter, after which he called again to say that the International Red Cross were on their way, but that they were held up overseeing the surrender of the Croatian soldiers and civilians in the sector south of Vukovar and that they would reach the hospital soon after. This was on the 18th. I believed that he was talking about the surrender or evacuation of Sajmiste. It was only later that I found out that he was in fact talking about the surrender and evacuation of Mitnica. It was at about 12.00 that the European monitors phoned me. This was the one and only time they did. They spoke to me in English and told me that they were sorry, that they were not able to come, that they were detained in the village of Negoslavci and that they would be there as soon as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I please apply for the tab 34 document to be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to move on to tab 36, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 35 in actual fact is a misprint. If my memory serves my correctly 35 relates to the 19th, not the 18th. Trying to do it chronologically. Sorry, perhaps I should have said that. So, 36, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn to page 76? This comes from 65 ter at number 996 and it's 0117/2554. This is a telephone message received at this page is both B/C/S and the English translation. We have got the name Vesna, Dr. Bosanac, there. It's received allegedly at 10.10 in the morning to the European mission. It's a short message. It says "artillery is attacking again. We were promised that the European mission would come this morning. We are being manipulated again." Now, this is apparently the 18th. Are you able to confirm whether you contacted presumably the Croatian liaison officer at the European mission on that day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the content itself, does it correspond with the conversation that you had?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't seeking to ask any questions about that, merely to make it an exhibit. It's part of a continued course of conduct through the 18th. So I'd make application for tab 36, please. I wonder could that be held back because tab 35 actually is the 19th, it's the very last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why don't you not move at the moment for its admission? We will deal with tab 35 if that is next. It's not next, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tab 35 actually is the 19th, not the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes but are you moving now to tab 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I'll go to 36, 37, then I will go to tab 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Look, we will make no decision about tab 36 at the moment. We will move again at an appropriate time, and we will now adjourn, given the time, resuming at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I move on, please, to tab 37? Tab 37 relates to phone messages on the 18th of November at 3.40 in the afternoon. They come from the 65 ter list 996 exhibit and 0117/2556.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn to page 77? And we will deal with page 78. This again is apparently a message received, telephone message received, apparently received by A. Kosovic. Would you, would you be kind enough, please, to read the content and confirm whether, in actual fact, it is of a nature and containing references that you were aware of, and indeed had communicated to A. Kosovic, if it was A. Kosovic who received it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that I transmitted this telephone message on the 18th of November at 15.40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you transmitted it to whom, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already told you, I kept calling the liaison office, with the European mission in Zagreb. I don't know who was on duty and who received the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, then, please, to look at the second one-sentence paragraph? And it seems to say, European Community/monitoring group for Vukovar made contact at 12.15 hours from Negoslavci. Their representative will come to the hospital if they allow him. Now, did you communicate that to the European monitoring mission?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I transmitted the message I received on the telephone from the monitors, the message to the effect that they were unable to come and that they would come to the hospital as soon as they were allowed to. This is what they told me. And then I in turn conveyed further this message about them not coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the phrase was, if they will allow him. How were they not able to come to Vukovar? The word "allow" is very specific.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first time I realised that, namely that they were unable to come on their own to Vukovar, if they wanted to. Instead, somebody else, in this case the Yugoslav People's Army, who had all roads leading to Vukovar under their control had to, prior to that, issue permission for them to travel to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it meets with the agreement or consent of the court, the documents that one can find on the index running from tab 35 to 39 clearly have been thrown out of sync by tab 35 being in the wrong place. I've mentioned to the court officer. I haven't had a chance to mention to my learned friends, but if in actual fact these documents are dealt with sequentially, as I intend to do, and there is no objection taken to them, then at the end of what I will call the tabbed documents, they can retain their original tab numbers which will then have that exhibit number and not create any problems at all. I'm entirely in the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will continue on until you've reached the end --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much indeed. But I would be making application for them to be made an exhibit. May I move, then, to tab 37, please? Tab 37 is a telephone message, 18th of November, sorry, my apologies, tab 39 would be the next one. And it is -- corresponds at the same time. So that's page 80 and page 81. They are from 65 ter 223, and it would be ZA004235 and 4236.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, doctor, looking at page 81, it seems to be the same nature of document; is that right? Well it is the same document itself, actually, but by a different route.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would ask that to be made an exhibit in due course. Then moving to tab 38, which is proceeding along on that day, in chronological form, it's a phone message then, approximately three hours later, it's page 79. It is ter 996, ERN number 0117/2557.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This, again, allegedly is a telephone call made by you, the timing clearly is in error on the translation. It is at 18.55, which would be 6.55 in the evening, but the document says 4.55, but if I just move on, apart from that, in relation to the message, would you be kind enough, please, to just look at who it's addressed to? It seems to be the European mission. Is that exactly the same route that you have taken on previous occasions?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that in actual fact, we have got Dr. Vesna Bosanac, bottom right-hand corner? Again would you be kind enough to read the content of this document and see if it corresponds with a telephone conversation that you had in the late afternoon of the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to look at the very bottom paragraph starting, "We implore for an urgent help and arrival of the representatives of the EC mission and International Red Cross respectively without Yugoslav army escort as there are no Croatian army within the hospital surrounding as we were required by the EC mission?" Now, what did you mean by that, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evacuation was discussed prior to that, as I have told you. I talked to Minister Hebrang and he asked me whether there were any Croatian soldiers in the vicinity of the hospital. I told him that there were none. I said that there were just the wounded there, and those who were assigned by the Croatian army to protect the hospital. I thought that I -- if I phrased it in those terms I would speed up the arrival of European monitors and the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will make application for that to be made an exhibit. And then finally at tab 35. And this is the 19th of November, tab 35, an apparent phone call made at 9.00 in the morning, 1 minute past 9.00. It's ter number 996 0117/2555.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you got that, Doctor? Page 75, top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again, from the medical centre Vukovar, apparently a telephone message, received the European mission, I'm not going to ask that question any more. And Dr. Bosanac is the name. I'll read it out. "We are calling today on the 19th of November 1991 at 1 minute past 9.00 that nobody called by phone yet or came in person in connection with the agreed evacuation." When we see "agreed evacuation," what did you mean on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed prior to that, by Minister Hebrang, as I've already told you, that an agreement had been signed, an agreement on evacuation of the wounded from the hospital. This is therefore what I had in mind, that agreement and the evacuation that had been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Can you just inform us what exactly the situation was on the 19th in the hospital? We have now finished with all these documents and I will seek to make them exhibits but before I do that, can you just answer this one question? What was it like on the 19th, when you sent that telephone message?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was very grave. The hospital was full of the wounded. The ill people, civilians who arrived from nearby shelters and basements. The situation was grave indeed. We had no more food, water, medicine, as I've mentioned several times already. We were hoping for an evacuation. However, nothing was going on at the time when I sent this telephone message to the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I then formally apply for tabs 35 to 39 inclusive? And I'll separate them out for documentation. So tab 35 we make application for it to be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tab 36, the document in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received as Exhibit number 36.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tab 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, as I see them, Mr. Moore, tab 37 and tab 39 are the identical document but somehow two slightly different translations appear, one with each. I would think don't need both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we will have 38 and not 39. Is that it? You've already got 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was just thinking, yes, I agree. Thank you very much for that. And then tab 35 -- sorry, 39, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 39 we won't exhibit because the original document is identical with that in 37. We do receive Exhibit 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. That concludes the material in what I call tabulated form for faxes. Can I just then move on to one or two different areas? Your Honour with regard to the hard copy, I want to now deal with the evacuation agreement. That is at index 1, but it is certainly with the E-Court system and it may well be deemed appropriate for it to go into E-Court at this stage. So what I was going to do was to deal with the rest of the documents that I have and there aren't very many, to deal with it by way of E-Court. I don't know if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if I can deal with it in this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, you have told us about the belief that there was an evacuation agreement in place. Would you be kind enough to look at a document which has been given the title, "The Zagreb evacuation document", the number is 00072600 for the assistance of E-Court. Now, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did you actually see the document for the first time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I left the prison in December of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to deal with things in a slightly unusual way by jumping ahead in time. I think it's right that you yourself, after the hospital was evacuated, on the 21st of -- 20th, 21st of November, you were taken to, as you describe it, prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the evacuation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When were you actually taken away?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where were you taken to eventually?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was first taken to the barracks of the Yugoslav army in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right you eventually ended up at Sremska Mitrovica; is that right, in a camp?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the night, between the 20th and the 21st, I was transported from the barracks in Vukovar to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, when you were at -- I'll call it prison because that's the word you used, when you were held in that camp or prison, how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And during that time, did you compile a document giving an account of what had happened to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the statement itself, is it in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you wrote it, were matters fresh in your memory?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Fresher than today?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, and I'm about to ask you to give evidence about what had happened at the hospital principally from the 18th to the 21st of November. Would it assist you with the Court's leave to refresh your memory from that document? So if there are parts that you can't remember by way of question, you can refer to the document to assist your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But actually I did not quite understand your question, the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. You wrote a document when you were at Sremska Mitrovica. It's in your handwriting, is that right? It was written some weeks, days and weeks, after you had come from the Vukovar Hospital. Do you follow so far?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in the document, you refer to places, occurrences, names, various details of what happened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions today, 15 years after the event, I'm asking whether, if in actual fact we use the phrase refresh your memory to look at the document if you need to to help you remember what occurred.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can take a look at the document, but I would rather not, because everything that happened to me during those last few days, both at the hospital and in prison, is something that I do not like to go back in my mind happily, but if you wish me to, I can go over that document and refresh my memory, if that is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I won't deal with the document at the moment. We will stick to the Zagreb agreement. Would you be kind enough, please, to look at paragraph 3 of the agreement? Because it deals with a route. Have you got that? Could you keep your voice up a little, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. It reads as follows: The convoy will take a route from Vukovar to Priljevo. Do you see that? And then gives a route itself.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the route that was actually taken, did you speak to any person about whether that was the route to take or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on the day of the evacuation or earlier? I did speak about that route to Minister Hebrang on an earlier occasion, and I also spoke to General Raseta. On the 19th of November I spoke to Colonel Mrksic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can we deal with your conversation with Colonel Mrksic please? You say that was when?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was this route discussed or a route discussed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed the evacuation. In our conversation, I described to him the situation at the hospital, and asked for the evacuation to commence as quickly as possible. He told me there were several ways to evacuate, through Sid, through Lipovac, and Professor Hebrang had already told me that a route had been agreed on, the following route, Luzac-Bogdanovci-Marinci-Nustar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you then take the route or did you take a different route for the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go. The hospital didn't go. The wounded and everyone else were evacuated along a different route, or at least that's what I heard. So that they passed through Sremska Mitrovica rather than the agreed route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you remember the explanation given to you by Colonel Mrksic of why it was that route couldn't be taken, it had to be changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: An element of it does appear to be, Mr. Moore. For the most part it isn't. It's the suggestion that the route had to be changed. Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, might I respectfully submit that there is reference to a conversation with Colonel Mrksic and if one looks at 61:01:13:23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A different route. It's the word "had" which you put in your last question. Instead of "was".

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll ask the question in a different way, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That may well help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The route that has been chosen, as far as you were aware, was that route the route that they actually took?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was any explanation given to you by anyone why you went on a different route?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked to Colonel Mrksic we discussed a number of possible evacuation routes. He listed some of those that he deemed possible. I told him that a route had already been agreed on and signed in Zagreb. The following route: Hospital-Luzac-Bogdanovci-Marinci-Vinkovci. He said this might prove a problem, because mines would have to be cleared from Zidine - Zidine is a place - and this was the reason that no evacuation could start on the 19th, but, rather, one would have to be organised on the following day, the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I ask you, please, to go to number 5? It reads "the evacuation will include all those wounded or sick undergoing medical treatment in Vukovar Hospital who are judged by the authorities of the hospital to be fit to make the journey." Now, I underline the word "all". Did that correspond or not with your understanding of what was to be agreed? Or to be followed is perhaps a better way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our understanding was that everyone would be evacuated from the hospital. We had a list containing the names of all the wounded who had specified their wish as to which part of Croatia, Yugoslavia, they wanted to be evacuated to, seeing as some of them had families in Zagreb or in Croatia's free territory. Some had requested to go to Belgrade or Novi Sad. At any rate, our expectation certainly was that all would be evacuated. As the hospital demolished as it was, and left with no infrastructure in place, could not continue to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you then, please, to look at paragraph 7, that really deals with the control of the evacuation. "The Republic of Croatia and YPA agree that the EC monitor mission should monitor the whole of the operation, having full access to all elements of the evacuation. The two parties will also facilitate the involvement of the ICRC, Medecins Sans Frontieres, and the Maltese Cross as appropriate to allow them to play such roles as may be decided in supporting and monitoring the evacuation. "You have told us that you had had telephone calls on the 18th of November in relation to the proposed evacuation that you were expecting Red Cross convoys. What was your understanding in relation to the control that was to be exercised by the monitors themselves, when it came to the evacuation of all the people --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected that the evacuation would be conducted in much the same way as one month before, the evacuation that had been organised by the Medecins Sans Frontieres. That the International Red Cross would be conducting the evacuation with the assistance of the European monitors, that was my idea of what -- how the evacuation would unfold.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with this conversation that you had with Colonel Mrksic, the conversation that related to the change of route for whatever reason? In that conversation with Colonel Mrksic, was there any discussion between you and him about who was to control the evacuation, the involvement of the monitors, and who would be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that an agreement had been signed in Zagreb. On behalf of the Croatian government and on behalf of General Raseta who was representing the JNA, as well as on behalf of the ECMM. This agreement specified the exact modality and route to be taken by the evacuation. I told him that on the afternoon of the 19th, in Negoslavci when we talked. If I may be allowed to add something about the translation of this agreement? It says signed for the Republic of Croatia, a signature, and then an illegible signature, 18 over 11 signed for the JNA and then an illegible signature. This illegible handwritten signature belongs to Mr. Georges-Marie Chenu who at the time was head of the monitoring mission in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But with regard to the conversation with Colonel Mrksic, you've answered some of the question, but was there any discussion about the responsibility of the monitors in the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the agreement signed in Zagreb envisaged in great detail the options or, rather, the guidelines, as well as the route for this evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what about the role of the monitors, i.e., the European mission, Medecins Sans Frontieres, Maltese Cross. Who was going to control the evacuation? Was that discussed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I told him about the agreement. I had not myself seen the agreement before the evacuation but I had been informed of its details. That precisely was the reason why I had requested to go to Negoslavci. I herd from the soldier who was the first to come to the hospital that the European monitors and the International Red Cross were there in Negoslavci and that's why I asked to go to Negoslavci myself, to meet the European monitors. I expected that they would be the first to arrive at the hospital and not the representatives of the JNA. This is something that I shared with Colonel Mrksic. I told him this was the reason I had gone to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in relation to paragraph 5 of the agreement, which you had not seen when you went to see Colonel Mrksic, that of course refers to all the wounded and you've given evidence about that. Did you have any conversation with Colonel Mrksic about actually who was to be evacuated, whether it was going to be some or whether it was going to be all? Can you help us, please, the details of the discussion with Colonel Mrksic on this topic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that all were to be evacuated, all meaning all. The hospital was facing a difficult situation. There was no water. Everything was filthy. Gangrene was rife. There were no medications. And all were to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Mrksic express any concerns or reservations about all being taken from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My understanding at the time was as follows. He said that the situation was now better because the shooting had ceased. He said we would now be better able to conduct an evacuation. Nevertheless, he himself did not know exactly what it was that General Raseta had signed in Zagreb. Raseta was in Zagreb and not on the ground. That would be a rough rendition of his words at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Mrksic at any time indicate that he would contact General Raseta to clarify exactly what the terms would be for the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This isn't something that he told me, or at least I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to go on to a specific topic that takes a little time. When I say a little time, it will take half an hour, I would have thought. I wonder if it would be possible to rise five minutes early and deal with that topic in one fell swoop? I can start it, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be more practical to break now, and come to this topic fresh tomorrow morning. Is there any other matter before we rise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that's the case, then, we will adjourn now to resume at 9.00 a.m. tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of October, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 25
